GuardFall Exposes Open-Source AI Coding Agents to Decades-Old Shell Injection Risks

The Hacker News
2026-06-30 10 use cases 5 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

The safety check that is supposed to stop an AI coding agent from running a dangerous command can be walked straight past using a shell trick that has been public for decades. New research from&nbsp;Adversa AI, which is named the bypass GuardFall, found it works against ten of the eleven popular open-source coding and computer-use agents the firm tested. Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Untrusted in-repo AI agent config (.aider.conf.yml) landing from clone/checkout · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Shell blocklist bypass via empty-quote/token-split binary names (GuardFall) · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Open-source AI coding agent auto-execute flag spawning a shell · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] AI agent shell reaching into ~/.ssh / ~/.aws credential files · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Shell blocklist bypass via empty-quote/token-split binary names (GuardFall) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts AI-coding-agent-spawned shells running commands obfuscated to defeat plain-text blocklists: empty-quote/backslash-split binary names (r''m), base64 piped into sh/bash, or benign tools (find/dd) given destructive flags. This is the exact GuardFall evasion shape where bash rewrites the string after the agent's filter inspected it. Rationale: Uses the article's literal GuardFall evasion primitives (empty-quote split like r''m, base64-pipe-to-shell, destructive find/dd flags) anchored to the named open-source agent binaries as parents — the combination of agent-parent + shell-child + obfuscated cmdline is far higher-fidelity than any single clause. Cross-checked against: • https://adversa.ai/ • https://arxiv.org/pdf/2509.22040
ATT&CKT1027.010 T1140 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer legitimately running a build script that base64-decodes an embedded asset and pipes it to a shell installer
  • CI/dev tooling using find -delete to clean build artifacts
  • dd used for legitimate disk imaging by a sysadmin on a dev box
  • Shell aliases or generated scripts that happen to contain quote-adjacent tokens
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("npm run build","make ","cmake","docker build") and ProcessCommandLine has "-delete")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full ProcessCommandLine and decode any base64; confirm the parent is an AI coding agent and whether the session was non-interactive/auto-exec. Identify the repo/working dir the agent was pointed at. 2) Contain: kill the agent + shell processes, revoke and rotate any credentials reachable from $HOME (~/.ssh, ~/.aws), and quarantine the host from prod networks. 3) Hunt: review the triggering repo/PR (especially fork PRs and in-repo config like .aider.conf.yml) for the injected instruction; sweep other dev hosts for the same agent-parent + obfuscated-shell pattern.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("aider","goose","cline","plandex","opencode","open-interpreter","openhands","swe-agent","node","python","python3")
| where FileName in~ ("bash","sh","dash","zsh")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)([a-z])'{2,}[a-z]|base64\s+-d.*\|\s*(ba)?sh|\bdd\s+.+of=/dev/|find\s+.+-delete|find\s+.+-exec\s+rm"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("aider","goose","cline","plandex","opencode","open-interpreter","openhands","swe-agent","node","python","python3")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("bash","sh","dash","zsh")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)([a-z])'{2,}[a-z]|base64\s+-d.*\|\s*(ba)?sh|\bdd\s+.+of=/dev/|find\s+.+-delete|find\s+.+-exec\s+rm"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Open-source AI coding agent auto-execute flag spawning a shell AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the GuardFall precondition: a named open-source coding agent invoked with an auto-execute / skip-permissions flag (--auto-exec, --auto-run, --auto-test, --yes-always, dangerously-skip-permissions) that then spawns a shell or interpreter non-interactively. This is the unattended configuration that lets an injected command actually run. Rationale: Anchors on the article's explicit auto-execute flag names (--auto-exec/--auto-run/--auto-test/dangerously-skip-permissions) AND the named agent binaries spawning a shell — the unattended-execution precondition the article says must be true for the attack to land, making it a high-fidelity governance/posture alert. Cross-checked against: • https://adversa.ai/ • https://www.theregister.com/2026/04/01/claude_code_rule_cap_raises/
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1059
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment

  • Developer using --yes-always on their own local repo for a known refactor
  • Automated test harness invoking the agent with --auto-test against a sandboxed branch
  • Demo/eval scripts running an agent non-interactively in a throwaway container
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName has_any ("ci-runner","build-agent") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "--auto-test")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the agent run was sanctioned (internal trusted repo vs fork/external) and which repo/working dir it targeted; capture the child shell command lines. 2) Contain: if the repo source is untrusted or unknown, terminate the agent session and disable the auto-execute flag in the relevant wrapper/CI job; isolate the host pending review. 3) Hunt: enumerate all hosts/CI runners running these agents with auto-exec flags, and correlate forward to credential-file reads or outbound connections from the spawned shells.

AI agent shell reaching into ~/.ssh / ~/.aws credential files AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the GuardFall credential-theft payload: a shell or copy/transfer tool spawned by an AI coding agent that reads SSH keys, cloud credentials, or other home-folder secrets. Targets the article's stated impact — stealing 'SSH keys and cloud credentials to anything sitting in your home folder'. Rationale: Combines the article's named agent binaries as parent with the exact credential paths it calls out (SSH keys, AWS/cloud creds in $HOME) referenced by a read/copy/transfer child process — agent-spawned access to ~/.ssh or ~/.aws is well outside normal agent working-dir behaviour. Cross-checked against: • https://adversa.ai/ • https://arxiv.org/pdf/2509.22040
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1552.004 T1005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An agent legitimately tasked with configuring git over SSH or deploying via scp reading ~/.ssh/config
  • Developer-driven 'aws configure' or terraform run that the agent shells out to and which touches ~/.aws/credentials
  • Backup or dotfile-sync tooling invoked through the agent's shell
  • Agent reading ~/.docker/config.json to run an authorized image build
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("aws configure","git@","ssh -T","terraform") )
Response runbook
1) Triage: determine whether the credential access matched the task the user gave the agent; capture the destination of any subsequent cp/scp/curl. 2) Contain: immediately rotate the specific keys/credentials touched (SSH keypairs, AWS access keys, kube tokens) and revoke sessions; isolate the host. 3) Hunt: pivot to DeviceNetworkEvents/NetworkConnectIP4 from the same shell for outbound exfil shortly after the read, and review the source repo/PR that the agent was operating on.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("aider","goose","cline","plandex","opencode","open-interpreter","openhands","swe-agent","node","python","python3")
| where FileName in~ ("bash","sh","dash","zsh","cat","cp","tar","scp","curl","wget","base64")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\.ssh/id_(rsa|ed25519|ecdsa)|\.aws/credentials|\.config/gcloud|\.kube/config|\.netrc|\.docker/config\.json"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc

| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("aider","goose","cline","plandex","opencode","open-interpreter","openhands","swe-agent","node","python","python3")

Untrusted in-repo AI agent config (.aider.conf.yml) landing from clone/checkout AIDelivery Low
Hunts the GuardFall initial-access vector where a malicious agent config file shipped inside a repository (the article calls out .aider.conf.yml) is written to disk by a VCS/clone or the agent itself, which can trigger the attack on the first accepted edit. Treats in-repo agent config as untrusted code. Rationale: Uses the exact config filename the article names as untrusted-code (.aider.conf.yml) written by a clone/checkout or the agent — a focused hunting pivot for the supply-chain delivery step, kept low-confidence/hunting because legitimate repos also ship this file. Cross-checked against: • https://adversa.ai/blog/the-approval-prompt-is-lying-to-you-symlink-rce-in-five-ai-coding-agents-claude-code-cursor-antigravity-copilot-grok-build/
ATT&CKT1195.001 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem

  • Templating/scaffolding tools generating an aider config
  • CI checkout of an internal repo that ships the file by policy
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath has_any ("/internal-repos/","/trusted/"))

1) Triage: inspect the contents of the written .aider.conf.yml for embedded auto-run/auto-commit settings, shell hooks, or instructions, and identify the source repo/PR (especially fork PRs). 2) Contain: if the repo is untrusted/external, prevent the agent from running against it, move $HOME to a throwaway folder per the article's guidance, and disable auto-execute. 3) Hunt: correlate forward to agent-spawned shells (UC1/UC2) and credential reads (UC3) on the same host within the session window.

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

ToddyCat: your hidden email assistant. Part 2

Securelist (Kaspersky)

An in-depth analysis of Umbrij, a new tool used by the ToddyCat APT group to compromise corporate email communications in Gmail. The attack targeted OAuth authorization tokens, allowing threat actors to gain access to Google services.

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Umbrij command-line switches (-deepsearch / -runas-currentuser / -debugport / -domainAd / -savepdf) · [LLM] Chromium browser launched headless with --remote-debugging-port by a non-browser parent (STRD) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Article-specific behavioural hunt — ToddyCat: your hidden email assistant. Part 2
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Masquerading scheduled task 'KasperskyEndpointSecurityEDRAvp' launching a signed binary · [LLM] ToddyCat Umbrij DLL side-loading: signed host loading malicious log.dll/GoogleServices.dll from writable path · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Sideload-host binary connecting to Google OAuth/Gmail API endpoints (token exchange) · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Masquerading scheduled task 'KasperskyEndpointSecurityEDRAvp' launching a signed binary AIInstallation High
Hunts the persistence/launch step where ToddyCat created a scheduled task named KasperskyEndpointSecurityEDRAvp to run a digitally-signed sideload host. Kaspersky never creates a task with this name, so any occurrence of the string is malicious by definition. Rationale: Anchors on the exact masquerading task name 'KasperskyEndpointSecurityEDRAvp' called out in the article's Execution section; it is a fixed, unique string no legitimate product emits. Cross-checked Securelist part 2 and the ToddyCat series. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/toddycat-apt-umbrij-tool-and-oauth/120251/ • https://securelist.com/toddycat-apt-steals-email-data-from-outlook/118044/ • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0228/
ATT&CKT1053.005 T1036.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A SOC analyst manually re-creating the task name during IR reproduction/testing
  • An internal red-team emulating ToddyCat TTPs
  • A detection-content lab importing the IOC string into a test task
  • Documentation/scripts that reference the task name in comments being scanned by inventory tooling
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the scheduled task definition (Actions/Exec path) and the signed binary it launches; verify the signer and whether the path is a writable dir (Users\Public, Temp, vss). 2) Contain: disable/delete the task, isolate the host, and capture the launched binary + any same-folder DLL for analysis. 3) Hunt: pivot on the launched binary hash and folder across the fleet; check for the BDS.exe/log.dll sideload chain and Chromium remote-debugging launches on the same host within +/- 1h.
union
(DeviceProcessEvents | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | where ProcessCommandLine has "KasperskyEndpointSecurityEDRAvp" | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, Evidence=ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName),
(DeviceRegistryEvents | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | where RegistryKey has @"\TaskCache\" and RegistryKey has "KasperskyEndpointSecurityEDRAvp" | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, Evidence=RegistryKey, InitiatingProcessFileName)
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID in (4698, 4702, 4699)
| where EventData has "KasperskyEndpointSecurityEDRAvp"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, Activity, EventID, EventData

ToddyCat Umbrij DLL side-loading: signed host loading malicious log.dll/GoogleServices.dll from writable path AIInstallation High
Hunts the exact sideload pairs ToddyCat abused to launch Umbrij: BDSubWiz.exe/bds.exe loading log.dll, VSTestVideoRecorder.exe loading Microsoft.VisualStudio.QualityTools.VideoRecorderEngine.dll, and GoogleDesktop.exe loading GoogleServices.dll, when the module loads from a user-writable directory or matches the known log.dll hashes. Rationale: Uses the exact legitimate-host -> malicious-DLL pairs named in the article (BDSubWiz/bds.exe+log.dll, VSTestVideoRecorder+VideoRecorderEngine.dll, GoogleDesktop+GoogleServices.dll), plus the writable paths and log.dll/BDS.exe MD5s read directly from in-article screenshot image1.jpeg (4C39087.../22AAEB49... and 28CB7B26...). Writable-path constraint removes legitimate in-product loads. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/toddycat-apt-umbrij-tool-and-oauth/120251/ • https://media.kasperskycontenthub.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/43/2026/06/16200713/image1.jpeg • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0228/
ATT&CKT1574.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine Bitdefender ConnectAgent running BDSubWiz.exe from its real Program Files path (excluded by writable-path filter)
  • Visual Studio test runs loading VideoRecorderEngine.dll from the VS install directory
  • A legacy Google Desktop install in Program Files loading GoogleServices.dll
  • Security testing/EDR validation copying these binaries into a sandbox temp folder
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files (x86)"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the loaded DLL hash against the known IOCs and verify the host binary is running from Users\Public/Temp/vss rather than its vendor install path; check the DLL export (LogInit) and ConfuserEx markers. 2) Contain: isolate the host, quarantine the DLL and host binary, kill the process tree. 3) Hunt: from the host process, pivot to child Chromium launches with --remote-debugging-port and outbound connections to *.googleapis.com; sweep fleet for the same DLL hashes and the KasperskyEndpointSecurityEDRAvp task.
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("BDSubWiz.exe","bds.exe") and FileName =~ "log.dll")
     or (InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "VSTestVideoRecorder.exe" and FileName =~ "Microsoft.VisualStudio.QualityTools.VideoRecorderEngine.dll")
     or (InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "GoogleDesktop.exe" and FileName =~ "GoogleServices.dll")
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Users\Public\", @"\AppData\Local\Temp\", @"\Windows\Temp\", @"\Windows\vss\")
     or MD5 in~ ("4C39087E5229A70F0215AFB8B7083091","22AAEB4946BA6D2F2E27FEB7DBB295DE")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, Dll=FileName, DllPath=FolderPath, MD5, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any (@"\BDSubWiz.exe", @"\bds.exe", @"\VSTestVideoRecorder.exe", @"\GoogleDesktop.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any (@"\Users\Public\", @"\AppData\Local\Temp\", @"\Windows\Temp\", @"\Windows\vss\")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName

Umbrij command-line switches (-deepsearch / -runas-currentuser / -debugport / -domainAd / -savepdf) AIExploitation High
Hunts execution of the Umbrij tool by its distinctive command-line parameters documented in the article, including the example invocation of a renamed BDSubWiz.exe with -regex and -deepsearch. These switch names are unique to Umbrij. Rationale: Anchors on the verbatim Umbrij CLI parameters enumerated in the article's parameter table (-deepsearch, -runas-currentuser, -domainAd, -savepdf, -debugport, -browser). These switch spellings are tool-specific and not used by mainstream software, giving very high fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/toddycat-apt-umbrij-tool-and-oauth/120251/
ATT&CKT1528 T1134.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A bespoke internal automation tool that happens to use a -debugport plus -browser flag combination
  • Red-team replaying Umbrij invocations during an authorized engagement
  • An unrelated CLI utility using the generic -savepdf flag (mitigated by requiring the ToddyCat-specific switch set)
  • Developer testing of a custom .NET tool with similar argument naming
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the full command line and the executing binary; resolve which browser/path/port were targeted (-path, -browser, -debugport) and whether -runas-currentuser/-user indicates token impersonation. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the process, and revoke/rotate the affected user's Google OAuth sessions and tokens immediately. 3) Hunt: correlate with the parent sideload host (BDS.exe/log.dll), Chromium --remote-debugging-port launches, and outbound *.googleapis.com traffic on the same host and account.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("-deepsearch","-runas-currentuser","-domainAd","-savepdf")
   or (ProcessCommandLine has "-debugport" and ProcessCommandLine has "-browser")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine has_any ("-deepsearch","-runas-currentuser","-domainAd","-savepdf")
   or (CommandLine has "-debugport" and CommandLine has "-browser")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName

Chromium browser launched headless with --remote-debugging-port by a non-browser parent (STRD) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the core Shadow-Token-via-Remote-Debug step: Umbrij launches Chrome/Edge/Chromium with a remote debugging port (often headless) to drive the user's live Gmail session. Flags browser processes carrying --remote-debugging-port when spawned by the sideload hosts or run headless. Rationale: Built on the article's explicit description of launching a Chromium browser in headless mode and connecting via the remote debugging port; pairs the --remote-debugging-port flag with the article-specific sideload parents or the --headless evasion flag to suppress legitimate interactive debugging. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/toddycat-apt-umbrij-tool-and-oauth/120251/ • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0228/
ATT&CKT1185 T1528
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developers/QA running Selenium/Puppeteer/Playwright automation with --remote-debugging-port and --headless
  • CI build agents driving headless Chrome for screenshot or PDF generation
  • VS Code / IDE debugging a web app via the Chrome DevTools Protocol
  • Synthetic monitoring agents launching headless browsers
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\Microsoft VS Code" and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("node.exe","devenv.exe","chromedriver.exe","msedgedriver.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the parent process and folder — a CI/automation tool from a dev path is likely benign; a browser spawned by BDSubWiz/bds/GoogleDesktop or from Users\Public/Temp is malicious. Note the --remote-debugging-port value and target profile. 2) Contain: isolate host, terminate the browser and parent, and immediately revoke the user's Google sessions/refresh tokens and force re-auth. 3) Hunt: pivot to outbound *.googleapis.com / accounts.google.com connections from the same host/account and to the Umbrij CLI-switch and log.dll sideload detections.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","chromium.exe","brave.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "--remote-debugging-port"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("BDSubWiz.exe","bds.exe","VSTestVideoRecorder.exe","GoogleDesktop.exe")
     or ProcessCommandLine has "--headless"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any (@"\chrome.exe", @"\msedge.exe", @"\chromium.exe", @"\brave.exe")
| where CommandLine has "--remote-debugging-port"
| where ParentProcessName has_any (@"\BDSubWiz.exe", @"\bds.exe", @"\VSTestVideoRecorder.exe", @"\GoogleDesktop.exe")
     or CommandLine has "--headless"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName

| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Sideload-host binary connecting to Google OAuth/Gmail API endpoints (token exchange) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the credential-access/exfil step where Umbrij (running as a renamed signed binary, not a browser) exchanges the stolen OAuth authorization code for an access token and pulls Gmail via the Google API. Flags the sideload hosts contacting *.googleapis.com / accounts.google.com. Rationale: Combines the article's OAuth-code-to-access-token exchange and Google-API access with the sideload host names confirmed in screenshot image1.jpeg; a renamed Bitdefender/VSTest/GoogleDesktop binary speaking directly to Google OAuth/Gmail APIs (work normally done only by the browser) is a strong, low-FP anomaly. Sentinel left empty because process-attributed network telemetry to these hosts is not available in standard Sentinel tables (would require Sysmon EID3 ingestion). Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/toddycat-apt-umbrij-tool-and-oauth/120251/ • https://media.kasperskycontenthub.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/43/2026/06/16200713/image1.jpeg • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0228/
ATT&CKT1528 T1114.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A genuine Google Desktop legacy install (in Program Files) performing update/sync checks to googleapis.com
  • Bitdefender ConnectAgent telemetry/update traffic to a Google-hosted CDN (rare; mitigated by host-name + writable-path context)
  • Security testing of the binaries in a lab with live internet
  • A renamed-but-benign internal tool reusing one of these file names
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files (x86)"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the initiating binary path/signer and verify it is the renamed sideload host rather than the genuine vendor product; pull the destination URLs and timing relative to any browser remote-debug launch. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block the binary, and revoke the affected Google account's OAuth tokens/refresh tokens and active sessions; review Google Workspace audit logs for token grants and bulk message reads. 3) Hunt: enumerate other hosts where these binaries reach Google APIs, correlate with the log.dll sideload and KasperskyEndpointSecurityEDRAvp task, and check for mailbox data staged/exfiltrated.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("BDSubWiz.exe","bds.exe","VSTestVideoRecorder.exe","GoogleDesktop.exe")
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("oauth2.googleapis.com","accounts.google.com","www.googleapis.com","gmail.googleapis.com","googleapis.com")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("BDSubWiz.exe","bds.exe","VSTestVideoRecorder.exe","GoogleDesktop.exe")
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("oauth2.googleapis.com","accounts.google.com","www.googleapis.com","gmail.googleapis.com","googleapis.com")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: ToddyCat Sideload Host Contacting Google OAuth/Gmail API
id: e7b3c91d-5a42-4f8e-8c01-9d2f6a3b7e58
description: Detects a ToddyCat sideload-host binary (not a browser) making network connections to Google OAuth / Gmail API endpoints, indicating OAuth token exchange and remote mailbox access.
references:
  - https://securelist.com/toddycat-apt-umbrij-tool-and-oauth/120251/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/30
tags:
  - attack.t1528

logsource:
  category: network_connection

detection:

NETWORK

| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where (All_Traffic.process_name="BDSubWiz.exe" OR All_Traffic.process_name="bds.exe" OR All_Traffic.process_name="VSTestVideoRecorder.exe" OR All_Traffic.process_name="GoogleDesktop.exe") AND (All_Traffic.dest="*googleapis.com*" OR All_Traffic.dest="*accounts.google.com*") by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.process_name All_Traffic.dest_port

| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where (All_Traffic.process_name="BDSubWiz.exe" OR All_Traffic.process_name="bds.exe" OR All_Traffic.process_name="VSTestVideoRecorder.exe" OR All_Traffic.process_name="GoogleDesktop.exe") AND (All_Traffic.dest="*googleapis.com*" OR All_Traffic.dest="*accounts.google.com*") by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.process_name All_Traffic.dest_port

OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High
Cloud identity abuse: app gets high-priv scopes, often via consent phishing.
ATT&CKT1528 T1098.001
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication CloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("Consent to application.","Add OAuth2PermissionGrant.","Add delegated permission grant.")
| project Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, ActivityType,
          ActivityObjects, IPAddress, UserAgent
// Entra ID directory audit — user / admin consent to a third-party app.
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("1AB58838E5790EFB22F2D35AB98C0B7D", "A7D7D6C4C3F227F7117261C63B9E23A9", "3D3A621F852C42D97FD7260681E42508", "3432DD9AC0DF80EF86EB80BD080F839B", "22AAEB4946BA6D2F2E27FEB7DBB295DE", "F61FBFB7AA1CD5DC8F70B055B51563E2", "F169D6D172DFB775895A5E2B1540C854", "9F5F2F0FB0A7F5AA9F16B9A7B6DAD89F", "28CB7B261F4EB97E8A4B3B0D32F8DEF1", "BAE82A15D1DBFB024617B9B56A8E5F66") or SHA1 in~ ("1AB58838E5790EFB22F2D35AB98C0B7D", "A7D7D6C4C3F227F7117261C63B9E23A9", "3D3A621F852C42D97FD7260681E42508", "3432DD9AC0DF80EF86EB80BD080F839B", "22AAEB4946BA6D2F2E27FEB7DBB295DE", "F61FBFB7AA1CD5DC8F70B055B51563E2", "F169D6D172DFB775895A5E2B1540C854", "9F5F2F0FB0A7F5AA9F16B9A7B6DAD89F", "28CB7B261F4EB97E8A4B3B0D32F8DEF1", "BAE82A15D1DBFB024617B9B56A8E5F66") or MD5 in~ ("1AB58838E5790EFB22F2D35AB98C0B7D", "A7D7D6C4C3F227F7117261C63B9E23A9", "3D3A621F852C42D97FD7260681E42508", "3432DD9AC0DF80EF86EB80BD080F839B", "22AAEB4946BA6D2F2E27FEB7DBB295DE", "F61FBFB7AA1CD5DC8F70B055B51563E2", "F169D6D172DFB775895A5E2B1540C854", "9F5F2F0FB0A7F5AA9F16B9A7B6DAD89F", "28CB7B261F4EB97E8A4B3B0D32F8DEF1", "BAE82A15D1DBFB024617B9B56A8E5F66")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("1AB58838E5790EFB22F2D35AB98C0B7D", "A7D7D6C4C3F227F7117261C63B9E23A9", "3D3A621F852C42D97FD7260681E42508", "3432DD9AC0DF80EF86EB80BD080F839B", "22AAEB4946BA6D2F2E27FEB7DBB295DE", "F61FBFB7AA1CD5DC8F70B055B51563E2", "F169D6D172DFB775895A5E2B1540C854", "9F5F2F0FB0A7F5AA9F16B9A7B6DAD89F", "28CB7B261F4EB97E8A4B3B0D32F8DEF1", "BAE82A15D1DBFB024617B9B56A8E5F66") or SHA1 in~ ("1AB58838E5790EFB22F2D35AB98C0B7D", "A7D7D6C4C3F227F7117261C63B9E23A9", "3D3A621F852C42D97FD7260681E42508", "3432DD9AC0DF80EF86EB80BD080F839B", "22AAEB4946BA6D2F2E27FEB7DBB295DE", "F61FBFB7AA1CD5DC8F70B055B51563E2", "F169D6D172DFB775895A5E2B1540C854", "9F5F2F0FB0A7F5AA9F16B9A7B6DAD89F", "28CB7B261F4EB97E8A4B3B0D32F8DEF1", "BAE82A15D1DBFB024617B9B56A8E5F66") or MD5 in~ ("1AB58838E5790EFB22F2D35AB98C0B7D", "A7D7D6C4C3F227F7117261C63B9E23A9", "3D3A621F852C42D97FD7260681E42508", "3432DD9AC0DF80EF86EB80BD080F839B", "22AAEB4946BA6D2F2E27FEB7DBB295DE", "F61FBFB7AA1CD5DC8F70B055B51563E2", "F169D6D172DFB775895A5E2B1540C854", "9F5F2F0FB0A7F5AA9F16B9A7B6DAD89F", "28CB7B261F4EB97E8A4B3B0D32F8DEF1", "BAE82A15D1DBFB024617B9B56A8E5F66")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["1AB58838E5790EFB22F2D35AB98C0B7D", "A7D7D6C4C3F227F7117261C63B9E23A9", "3D3A621F852C42D97FD7260681E42508", "3432DD9AC0DF80EF86EB80BD080F839B", "22AAEB4946BA6D2F2E27FEB7DBB295DE", "F61FBFB7AA1CD5DC8F70B055B51563E2", "F169D6D172DFB775895A5E2B1540C854", "9F5F2F0FB0A7F5AA9F16B9A7B6DAD89F", "28CB7B261F4EB97E8A4B3B0D32F8DEF1", "BAE82A15D1DBFB024617B9B56A8E5F66"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Chromium extension uses AI‑related branding to redirect browser search

Microsoft Security Blog
2026-06-29 10 use cases 3 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

A malicious Chromium-based extension that spoofs the AI-powered answer engine Perplexity AI redirects browser search traffic using MV3 APIs and intermediary infrastructure. The post Chromium extension uses AI‑related branding to redirect browser search appeared first on Microsoft Security Blog .

ATT&CKT1176 T1190 T1566
Domainsperplexity-ai.online oda.digital extension.tilda.ws

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Chromium extension uses AI‑related branding to redirect browser search
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Malicious Perplexity-spoofing extension ID flkebkiofojicogddingbdmcmkpbplcd written to disk · Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Search-interception traffic to Perplexity typosquat domain perplexity-ai[.]online · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
Search-interception traffic to Perplexity typosquat domain perplexity-ai[.]online AICommand & Control High
Hunts browser connections/DNS resolutions to the attacker-controlled search-interception infrastructure (perplexity-ai.online and related oda.digital / extension.tilda.ws) used by the fake 'Search for perplexity ai' Chromium extension. Because the extension routes every Omnibox query and keystroke-level suggestion through this domain before redirecting to a real engine, any browser-originated traffic to these hosts is high-fidelity evidence of an infected endpoint. Rationale: Anchored on the exact interception domain perplexity-ai.online (confirmed by both the MSFT blog and The Hacker News) plus the pre-extracted secondary infra oda.digital / extension.tilda.ws, scoped to browser parent processes — a typosquat domain reached by a browser is near-zero-FP. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/malicious-perplexity-chrome-extension.html • https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/search-for-perplexity-ai/flkebkiofojicogddingbdmcmkpbplcd • https://www.crx4chrome.com/extensions/flkebkiofojicogddingbdmcmkpbplcd/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1176 T1185
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SOC/IR analyst detonating the extension sample in a managed sandbox host
  • Web proxy / secure-web-gateway pre-fetching or URL-categorizing the domain on a user's behalf
  • Threat-intel enrichment or DNS-sinkhole tooling resolving the IOC for blocking
  • A user who clicked the lookalike landing page once but did not install (single browse vs. repeated query routing)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsMpEng.exe","MsSense.exe","SenseIR.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm which device/user generated the traffic and whether the 'Search for perplexity ai' extension (ID flkebkiofojicogddingbdmcmkpbplcd) is installed; check if default search provider was overridden to perplexity-ai.online. 2) Contain: force-remove the extension via browser policy/ExtensionInstallBlocklist, reset the default search engine, and block perplexity-ai.online / oda.digital / extension.tilda.ws at proxy and DNS. 3) Hunt: pivot on all other hosts resolving these domains and review browsing/search history routed through the domain for sensitive query exposure during the exposure window.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("perplexity-ai.online","oda.digital","extension.tilda.ws")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe","vivaldi.exe","chrome_proxy.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Name has_any ("perplexity-ai.online","oda.digital","extension.tilda.ws")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, ResultCode, ResultCodeName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Malicious Perplexity-spoofing extension ID flkebkiofojicogddingbdmcmkpbplcd written to disk AIInstallation High
Hunts for the unique Chrome Web Store extension ID flkebkiofojicogddingbdmcmkpbplcd ('Search for perplexity ai') appearing in browser extension folder paths or written files on managed endpoints. The extension ID is a globally unique 32-char identifier, so any file-system artifact bearing it is a deterministic indicator that the taken-down malicious search hijacker was installed. Rationale: The 32-char extension ID flkebkiofojicogddingbdmcmkpbplcd is a globally unique store identifier (confirmed via the Chrome Web Store and crx4chrome listings), so its presence in any extension folder path is a deterministic install indicator with effectively no collisions. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/malicious-perplexity-chrome-extension.html • https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/search-for-perplexity-ai/flkebkiofojicogddingbdmcmkpbplcd • https://www.crx4chrome.com/extensions/flkebkiofojicogddingbdmcmkpbplcd/
ATT&CKT1176 T1185
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Endpoint backup software capturing the Chrome 'User Data' profile directory that still contains the extension folder
  • IR/forensic collection tooling copying browser profiles for offline analysis
  • AV/EDR scanning or quarantining the extension folder (file-access touches the path)
  • Sync of an already-infected profile to a new device via Chrome profile sync before takedown
Suppression filter
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed","FileModified") and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsMpEng.exe","MsSense.exe","SenseIR.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the ActionType (FileCreated = fresh install vs FileDeleted = remediation) and identify the user profile and browser hosting the extension folder. 2) Contain: remove the extension, push it to the browser ExtensionInstallBlocklist policy, and reset the hijacked default search provider; block perplexity-ai.online at DNS/proxy. 3) Hunt: correlate with UC1 network telemetry to confirm queries were exfiltrated, and sweep the fleet for the same extension ID to find all installs.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath has "flkebkiofojicogddingbdmcmkpbplcd"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, FileOriginUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFilePath has "flkebkiofojicogddingbdmcmkpbplcd"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, DvcAction, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;

The Gentlemen network sniffing via netsh trace capture redirected to ADMIN$ share AIReconnaissance High
Hunts The Gentlemen's reconnaissance technique of running netsh trace packet capture and writing the .etl output across the network to a remote host's ADMIN$ share. The redirect of a netsh trace start/stop session to \\<ip>\ADMIN$\ is highly specific to this actor's credential-harvesting-from-the-wire workflow. Rationale: Built from the article's exact commands 'netsh trace start capture=yes report=no filemode=circular overwrite=yes maxSize=4 > \\<target IP>\ADMIN$\{RANDOM}' and the matching 'netsh trace stop' redirect. netsh trace + ADMIN$ redirect is rare in benign admin use, making this high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/25/i/unmasking-the-gentlemen-ransomware.html • https://www.huntress.com/blog/the-gentlemen-ransomware-defense-evasion-ttps
ATT&CKT1040 T1059.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Network engineer running netsh trace for legitimate troubleshooting and saving to a local file (no ADMIN$ redirect)
  • Endpoint support tooling that captures ETL traces locally
  • Microsoft support diagnostic scripts (TSS toolkit) invoking netsh trace
  • Vendor performance-monitoring agents starting circular ETW captures
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("\\TSS\\", "TSSv2") and AccountName endswith "admin")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the redirect target — a \\<remote-ip>\ADMIN$ path means cross-host write, not local troubleshooting. Identify the executing account and whether it is an admin/service account that does not normally run netsh. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the source host, reset the credentials of the executing account, and pull the dropped .etl from the target ADMIN$ share for analysis (it may contain cleartext creds). 3) HUNT: Search for SharpADWS/NetScan/Advanced IP Scanner activity, the deploy_gpo.ps1 script, and connections to 81.177.215.15:9443 on the same hosts.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "netsh" and ProcessCommandLine has "trace"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("capture=yes", @"\ADMIN$\")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| where CommandLine has "netsh" and CommandLine has "trace"
| where CommandLine has_any ("capture=yes", "\\ADMIN$\\")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

The Gentlemen Go backdoor C2 beacon to 81.177.215.15 on TCP/9443 AICommand & Control Medium
Alerts on any host establishing an outbound connection to the confirmed Gentlemen Go-backdoor C2 IP 81.177.215.15 on port 9443, the Yamux-multiplexed persistent channel used for remote command execution and SOCKS proxying. Single confirmed C2 indicator deployed a day before ransomware. Rationale: Uses the article's explicit C2 endpoint 81.177.215.15:9443 for the Yamux-based Go backdoor. A hardcoded malicious IP+port is a high-confidence, near-zero-FP network IOC. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/05/28/the-gentlemen-ransomware-dissecting-a-self-propagating-go-encryptor/ • https://s2w.inc/en/resource/detail/1053
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1571 T1090
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researchers/sandbox detonating the sample from corporate ranges
  • Threat-intel scanning or Shodan-style internet measurement hitting the IP
  • Reused VPS IP later assigned to a benign service (validate against current TI reputation)
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Identify the InitiatingProcess making the connection — a Go binary in an unusual path (Temp/Public/AppData) deployed ~1 day prior is the backdoor. Capture its SHA256 against the article's hash list. 2) CONTAIN: Network-isolate the host, block 81.177.215.15 at the perimeter, and kill/quarantine the implant binary. 3) HUNT: Look for WMI query 'SELECT UUID FROM Win32_ComputerSystemProduct', cmd.exe /c children of the implant (operator command 'c'), SOCKS proxy listeners, and expect ransomware staging within ~24h.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "81.177.215.15" and RemotePort == 9443
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessSHA256, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr == "81.177.215.15" and DstPortNumber == 9443
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, DvcAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

The Gentlemen BYOVD vulnerable driver drop/load (EDR-killer drivers) AIInstallation High
Hunts for the specific vulnerable kernel drivers The Gentlemen abuse in their BYOVD/GentleKiller workflow to terminate security products. Matches on the named .sys files being written or loaded, e.g. biontdrv.sys, wamsdk.sys, ProcessMonitorDriver.sys. Rationale: Driver names taken verbatim from the article's vulnerable-driver table (Safetica, WatchDog, Paragon biontdrv, inpoutx64, etc.). ESET's GentleKiller research corroborates these as the actor's BYOVD arsenal. Medium FP because inpoutx64.sys/biontdrv.sys also appear in legitimate software. Cross-checked against: • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/killing-me-gently-inside-gentlemens-edr-killer-framework/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/gentlemen-ransomware-uses-multiple-edr-killers-to-disable-defenses/
ATT&CKT1562.001 T1068
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • inpoutx64.sys loaded by legitimate RGB-lighting/overclocking utilities
  • biontdrv.sys present from a genuine Paragon Partition Manager install
  • gamedriverx64.sys from a legitimately installed game with anti-cheat
  • Security product (Safetica) itself loading ProcessMonitorDriver.sys in an authorized deployment
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\Program Files\" and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("msiexec.exe","setup.exe","paragon.exe")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Check the signing status and the parent process that wrote/loaded the driver — a driver dropped to a non-standard path by a non-installer process is malicious; a vendor MSI installer is likely benign. Confirm whether the matching legitimate product is actually installed. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host, stop the driver service, and quarantine the .sys + the loading process; verify EDR/AV agents are still running. 3) HUNT: Correlate with Set-MpPreference tampering, OpenArk64/PowerRun.exe execution, and the 81.177.215.15 C2 on the same host to confirm Gentlemen activity.

| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("ProcessMonitorDriver.sys","wamsdk.sys","gamedriverx64.sys","biontdrv.sys","inpoutx64.sys","wsftprm.sys","Havoc.sys")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc

| where TargetFileName in~ ("ProcessMonitorDriver.sys","wamsdk.sys","gamedriverx64.sys","biontdrv.sys","inpoutx64.sys","wsftprm.sys","Havoc.sys")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine

id: 7e1b9d54-3a06-4c8e-9f21-6b5d0c2a4e8f
description: Detects load or write of vulnerable kernel drivers abused by The Gentlemen RaaS for EDR/AV termination (BYOVD).
references:
  - https://securelist.com/the-gentlemen-raas/120447/
  - https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/killing-me-gently-inside-gentlemens-edr-killer-framework/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/29
tags:
  - attack.t1562.001
  - attack.t1068
logsource:
  category: image_load
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    ImageLoaded|endswith:
      - '\ProcessMonitorDriver.sys'
      - '\wamsdk.sys'
      - '\gamedriverx64.sys'
      - '\biontdrv.sys'
      - '\inpoutx64.sys'
      - '\wsftprm.sys'
      - '\Havoc.sys'
  condition: selection
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 (@TargetFilename:*ProcessMonitorDriver.sys OR @TargetFilename:*processmonitordriver.sys OR @TargetFilename:*wamsdk.sys OR @TargetFilename:*gamedriverx64.sys OR @TargetFilename:*biontdrv.sys OR @TargetFilename:*inpoutx64.sys OR @TargetFilename:*wsftprm.sys OR @TargetFilename:*Havoc.sys OR @TargetFilename:*havoc.sys)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten
| TargetFileName=/(ProcessMonitorDriver|wamsdk|gamedriverx64|biontdrv|inpoutx64|wsftprm|Havoc)\.sys$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=t count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_name IN ("ProcessMonitorDriver.sys","wamsdk.sys","gamedriverx64.sys","biontdrv.sys","inpoutx64.sys","wsftprm.sys","Havoc.sys") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_name IN ("ProcessMonitorDriver.sys","wamsdk.sys","gamedriverx64.sys","biontdrv.sys","inpoutx64.sys","wsftprm.sys","Havoc.sys") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
The Gentlemen impair defenses via Set-MpPreference exclusions and AV-removal tooling AIInstallation High
Detects The Gentlemen's defense-evasion step that disables Defender real-time/CFA protection, adds whole-drive exclusions via Set-MpPreference/Add-MpPreference, and runs known AV-removal utilities (kavrmvr.exe, OpenArk64, PowerRun.exe, Allpatch2.exe). Pairs the Go-implant PowerShell cmdlets with named tampering binaries. Rationale: Combines the article's verbatim Go-implant cmdlets (Set-MpPreference -DisableRealtimeMonitoring, -EnableControlledFolderAccess Disabled, Add-MpPreference -ExclusionProcess/-ExclusionPath 'C:\') with named tools kavrmvr.exe (Kaspersky uninstaller) and OpenArk64; PowerRun.exe/Allpatch2.exe added from corroborating Trend Micro reporting on the same actor. Cross-checked against: • https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/25/i/unmasking-the-gentlemen-ransomware.html • https://www.huntress.com/blog/the-gentlemen-ransomware-defense-evasion-ttps
ATT&CKT1562.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT admin legitimately adding a Defender exclusion for a line-of-business app (single ExclusionPath, not C:\)
  • Sanctioned migration off Kaspersky running kavrmvr.exe with change-ticket approval
  • Performance team disabling Real-Time Monitoring temporarily during a benchmark
  • Software packaging/SCCM scripts setting exclusions for an installer
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has "ExclusionPath" and ProcessCommandLine !has @"'C:\'" and ProcessCommandLine !has "DisableRealtimeMonitoring" and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("ccmexec.exe","tiworker.exe"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Inspect the exclusion scope — a whole-drive 'C:\' exclusion or DisableRealtimeMonitoring chained with ExclusionProcess is malicious; a narrow app path may be benign. Identify the parent process (Go implant / cmd.exe /c). 2) CONTAIN: Re-enable Defender real-time protection and CFA, remove rogue exclusions, isolate the host, and reset the executing account. 3) HUNT: Pivot to BYOVD driver loads, registry Defender-policy keys, deploy_gpo.ps1, and the 81.177.215.15 C2 to scope the intrusion.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where (FileName in~ ("kavrmvr.exe","OpenArk64.exe","PowerRun.exe","Allpatch2.exe"))
    or (FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
        and ProcessCommandLine has "MpPreference"
        and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("DisableRealtimeMonitoring","EnableControlledFolderAccess Disabled","ExclusionProcess","ExclusionPath"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| where (NewProcessName has_any ("kavrmvr.exe","OpenArk64.exe","PowerRun.exe","Allpatch2.exe"))
    or (NewProcessName has_any ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
        and CommandLine has "MpPreference"
        and CommandLine has_any ("DisableRealtimeMonitoring","EnableControlledFolderAccess Disabled","ExclusionProcess","ExclusionPath"))
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: The Gentlemen Defender Tampering and AV-Removal Tooling
id: c2f7a930-5b84-41de-9a17-8d6e3f01b4a2
description: Detects Defender real-time/CFA disabling and whole-drive exclusions via Set-MpPreference/Add-MpPreference, plus known AV-removal binaries used by The Gentlemen.
references:
  - https://securelist.com/the-gentlemen-raas/120447/
  - https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/25/i/unmasking-the-gentlemen-ransomware.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/29
tags:
  - attack.t1562.001
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_tools:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\kavrmvr.exe'
      - '\OpenArk64.exe'
      - '\PowerRun.exe'
      - '\Allpatch2.exe'
  selection_ps:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\powershell.exe'
      - '\pwsh.exe'
    CommandLine|contains|all:
      - 'MpPreference'
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'DisableRealtimeMonitoring'
      - 'EnableControlledFolderAccess Disabled'
      - 'ExclusionProcess'
      - 'ExclusionPath'
  condition: selection_tools or selection_ps
level: high
source:windows.security @EventID:4688 ((@Image:*\kavrmvr.exe OR @Image:*\KAVRMVR.EXE OR @Image:*\OpenArk64.exe OR @Image:*\openark64.exe OR @Image:*\PowerRun.exe OR @Image:*\powerrun.exe OR @Image:*\Allpatch2.exe OR @Image:*\allpatch2.exe) OR (@CommandLine:*MpPreference* AND (@CommandLine:*DisableRealtimeMonitoring* OR @CommandLine:*ExclusionProcess* OR @CommandLine:*ExclusionPath*)))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| (ImageFileName=/\\(kavrmvr|OpenArk64|PowerRun|Allpatch2)\.exe$/i OR (CommandLine=/MpPreference/i CommandLine=/(DisableRealtimeMonitoring|EnableControlledFolderAccess\s+Disabled|ExclusionProcess|ExclusionPath)/i))
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=t count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name IN ("kavrmvr.exe","OpenArk64.exe","PowerRun.exe","Allpatch2.exe") OR (Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") AND Processes.process="*MpPreference*" AND (Processes.process="*DisableRealtimeMonitoring*" OR Processes.process="*EnableControlledFolderAccess Disabled*" OR Processes.process="*ExclusionProcess*" OR Processes.process="*ExclusionPath*"))) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name IN ("kavrmvr.exe","OpenArk64.exe","PowerRun.exe","Allpatch2.exe") OR (Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") AND Processes.process="*MpPreference*" AND (Processes.process="*DisableRealtimeMonitoring*" OR Processes.process="*EnableControlledFolderAccess Disabled*" OR Processes.process="*ExclusionProcess*" OR Processes.process="*ExclusionPath*"))) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
The Gentlemen Windows Defender disabled via Policy registry keys AIInstallation High
Detects The Gentlemen disabling Defender by writing the policy registry values DisableAntiSpyware / DisableBehaviorMonitoring / DisableOnAccessProtection / DisableScanOnRealtimeEnable = 1 under the Windows Defender policy hive (via .reg import). Distinct registry-telemetry pivot from the PowerShell-based tampering. Rationale: Registry keys and values are taken verbatim from the article's exported .reg block under HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows Defender. Value-name + data=1 under the policy hive is high-fidelity tampering. Falcon left empty: these policy keys are not reliably captured by the AsepValueUpdate (autostart) event the FDR exposes. Cross-checked against: • https://www.huntress.com/blog/the-gentlemen-ransomware-defense-evasion-ttps • https://s2w.inc/en/resource/detail/1053
ATT&CKT1562.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Group Policy legitimately disabling Defender on hosts managed by a third-party AV (DisableAntiSpyware pushed by GPO)
  • Gold-image build process turning off Defender before installing the enterprise AV
  • Admin troubleshooting an AV conflict by temporarily setting DisableBehaviorMonitoring
  • MDM/SCCM baseline applying a Defender configuration
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("gpscript.exe","svchost.exe","ccmexec.exe","WmiPrvSE.exe")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm whether a sanctioned GPO/MDM pushed the value (InitiatingProcess = svchost/gpscript) versus an interactive process like reg.exe/regedit/cmd.exe run by a user. Check if a different enterprise AV is the intended owner. 2) CONTAIN: Revert the registry values, force a gpupdate, isolate the host if the writer was interactive/non-admin. 3) HUNT: Correlate same-host BYOVD driver loads, Set-MpPreference tampering, and C2 to 81.177.215.15:9443; expect ransomware staging shortly after.
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("RegistryValueSet","RegistryKeyCreated")
| where RegistryKey has @"\Policies\Microsoft\Windows Defender"
| where RegistryValueName in~ ("DisableAntiSpyware","DisableBehaviorMonitoring","DisableOnAccessProtection","DisableScanOnRealtimeEnable")
| where RegistryValueData == "1"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where RegistryKey has @"\Policies\Microsoft\Windows Defender"
| where RegistryValue in~ ("DisableAntiSpyware","DisableBehaviorMonitoring","DisableOnAccessProtection","DisableScanOnRealtimeEnable")
| where RegistryValueData in ("1","0x1","DWORD (0x00000001)")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, RegistryKey, RegistryValue, RegistryValueData, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: The Gentlemen Windows Defender Disabled via Policy Registry Keys
id: a51d3c8b-2f47-4e90-bb13-7c0a9e6d4f25
