PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command Exploitation High
Encoded or obfuscated PowerShell — common across loaders, recon, and post-exploitation.
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName,
          CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Obfuscated / Encoded PowerShell Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d08
status: experimental
description: |
    PowerShell launched with -EncodedCommand, base64 strings, hidden
    window, no-profile, bypass policy, IEX / Invoke-Expression / Net
    .WebClient.DownloadString — combinations indicating evasion.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1027
    - attack.execution
    - attack.defense-evasion
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_image:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
    selection_args:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '-enc '
            - 'EncodedCommand'
            - 'FromBase64String'
            - 'Invoke-Expression'
            - 'IEX('
            - 'DownloadString'
            - 'Net.WebClient'
            - '-w hidden'
            - '-WindowStyle Hidden'
            - '-nop'
            - '-NoProfile'
            - '-ep bypass'
            - '-ExecutionPolicy Bypass'
    condition: selection_image and selection_args
falsepositives:
    - DevOps tooling that legitimately uses encoded command for
      cross-shell escaping
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1195
    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor
falsepositives:
    - Many — installers and updaters legitimately spawn children. Pin
      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.
level: medium
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Article-specific behavioural hunt — ESET takes part in Operation Endgame to disrupt Amadey and Stealc Exploitation High
Auto-generated hunt targeting the specific binaries, paths, registry locations and command-line fragments named in this article. Hunting tier — needs analyst review and environment tuning before promotion to alerting.
ATT&CKT1547.001 T1547.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Registry
// Article-specific bespoke detection — ESET takes part in Operation Endgame to disrupt Amadey and Stealc
// Hunts the actual binaries / paths / commandline fragments named
// in the article instead of a generic technique-class template.

SystemSettings.exe executing from non-standard path (SharkLoader DLL side-load host) AIInstallation High
Hunts the legitimate Windows binary SystemSettings.exe running from anywhere other than C:\Windows\ImmersiveControlPanel\ (or WinSxS). StrikeShark copies this signed binary to C:\ProgramData\, vendor-named decoy dirs (e.g. KasperskyLab), and %APPDATA%\xwreg / %APPDATA%\xgdf to side-load the malicious SystemSettings.dll (SharkLoader). The relocated binary is the launch point of the whole Cobalt Strike chain. Rationale: Anchored on the article's exact relocation behaviour (copy SystemSettings.exe C:\ProgramData\, KasperskyLab/xwreg/xgdf decoy dirs). SystemSettings.exe only legitimately runs from ImmersiveControlPanel/WinSxS, making any other path near-deterministic for the side-load. Cross-checked against cybersecuritynews.com and cyberpress.org which confirm the SystemSettings.exe side-load and %APPDATA% working dirs. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/strikeshark-campaign/120326/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/hackers-use-cisco-anyconnect-and-google-update-lures/ • https://cyberpress.org/sharkloader-targets-global-governments/
ATT&CKT1574.002 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT admin manually copying SystemSettings.exe to a test/staging folder during Settings-app troubleshooting
  • Backup/imaging software shadowing the binary into a snapshot path that lacks the WinSxS marker
  • Security-product self-protection sandboxes that copy and re-execute system binaries
  • Application-virtualization layers (App-V/MSIX) that surface SystemSettings.exe from a redirected path
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("ccmexec.exe","msiexec.exe") and FolderPath has @"\ccmcache\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the FolderPath, SHA256, and parent of the relocated SystemSettings.exe; confirm a SystemSettings.dll exists in the SAME directory (legit copies never carry that DLL beside them) and check for DscCoreR.mui/SyncRes.dat siblings. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the process tree, and quarantine the directory; block the C2 domains (connect-microsoft.com, ms-record.com/.top, ms-tray.top) at the proxy/firewall. 3) Hunt: pivot on the parent (w3wp/java) for the originating webshell, and sweep the fleet for SystemSettings.exe in ProgramData/AppData plus the dual schtasks persistence.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "SystemSettings.exe"
| where FolderPath !startswith @"C:\Windows\ImmersiveControlPanel\" and FolderPath !has @"\WinSxS\"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith @"\SystemSettings.exe"
| where not(NewProcessName startswith @"C:\Windows\ImmersiveControlPanel\") and NewProcessName !has @"\WinSxS\"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: SystemSettings.exe Executed From Non-Standard Path (SharkLoader Side-Load)
id: 5f1c8a4e-3b2d-4c9a-9f6e-7a1b2c3d4e5f
status: experimental
description: Detects the legitimate Windows SystemSettings.exe running outside its canonical ImmersiveControlPanel/WinSxS location, used by StrikeShark to side-load SystemSettings.dll (SharkLoader).
references:
  - https://securelist.com/strikeshark-campaign/120326/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/25
tags:
  - attack.t1574.002
  - attack.t1036.005
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    Image|endswith: '\SystemSettings.exe'
  filter_legit:
    Image|startswith:
      - 'C:\Windows\ImmersiveControlPanel\'
      - 'C:\Windows\WinSxS\'
  condition: selection and not filter_legit
falsepositives:
  - Admin manually copying SystemSettings.exe for troubleshooting
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\SystemSettings.exe OR *\systemsettings.exe OR *\SYSTEMSETTINGS.EXE) -@Image:(*\ImmersiveControlPanel\* OR *\immersivecontrolpanel\* OR *\WinSxS\* OR *\winsxs\*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\SystemSettings\.exe$/i
| NOT ImageFileName=/\\(ImmersiveControlPanel|WinSxS)\\/i
| table([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, CommandLine, ParentBaseFileName, SHA256HashData])
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="SystemSettings.exe" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process_path Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where NOT (like(process_path,"%\\Windows\\ImmersiveControlPanel\\%") OR like(process_path,"%\\Windows\\WinSxS\\%")) | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)` | table firstTime lastTime dest user process_name process_path process parent_process_name count
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="SystemSettings.exe" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process_path Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where NOT (like(process_path,"%\\Windows\\ImmersiveControlPanel\\%") OR like(process_path,"%\\Windows\\WinSxS\\%")) | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)` | table firstTime lastTime dest user process_name process_path process parent_process_name count
SharkLoader encrypted payload files dropped (DscCoreR.mui + SyncRes.dat + SystemSettings.dll) AIInstallation High
Hunts creation of SharkLoader's distinctive component set in user-writable directories: the side-loaded SystemSettings.dll plus the encrypted in-memory-only modules DscCoreR.mui (Blowfish-decrypted) and SyncRes.dat (AES-128-decrypted API-hooking DLL). These filenames co-located in ProgramData/AppData are a near-unique campaign fingerprint. Rationale: Uses the article's exact module names DscCoreR.mui (Blowfish) and SyncRes.dat (AES-128) plus the side-loaded SystemSettings.dll — corroborated by cybersecuritynews.com describing the same DscCoreR.mui→SyncRes.dat decryption chain. DscCoreR.mui/SyncRes.dat are non-Windows filenames so any user-writable occurrence is high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/strikeshark-campaign/120326/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/hackers-use-cisco-anyconnect-and-google-update-lures/
ATT&CKT1574.002 T1140
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A third-party DSC (Desired State Configuration) tool legitimately staging a DscCore localized resource into ProgramData
  • Backup software re-hydrating an AppData folder that already contained the artifacts during a prior incident
  • Security-vendor sample-collection writing copies of these files into a quarantine/AppData path
  • Developer test fixtures that happen to reuse the SyncRes.dat name (rare)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("msmpeng.exe","mssense.exe","sensendr.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the writing process (InitiatingProcessFileName) and whether all three components landed in one directory; hash SystemSettings.dll and check signing — SharkLoader's DLL is unsigned/forged. 2) Contain: isolate host, quarantine the directory, and capture a memory image (SyncRes.dat/Beacon are decrypted only in memory). 3) Hunt: pivot to the SystemSettings.exe process that loads the DLL, the schtasks persistence, and outbound beacons to the campaign C2 domains; sweep fleet for the same filename triad.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where FileName in~ ("SystemSettings.dll","DscCoreR.mui","SyncRes.dat")
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\ProgramData\", @"\AppData\", @"\Users\Public\")
| where not(FileName =~ "SystemSettings.dll" and FolderPath startswith @"C:\Windows\")
| summarize Components=make_set(FileName), Paths=make_set(FolderPath), DistinctComponents=dcount(FileName), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by LastSeen desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("SystemSettings.dll","DscCoreR.mui","SyncRes.dat")
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\ProgramData\", @"\AppData\", @"\Users\Public\")
| summarize Components=make_set(TargetFileName), Paths=make_set(TargetFilePath), DistinctComponents=dcount(TargetFileName), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated) by DvcHostname, ActingProcessName
| order by FirstSeen desc

Web server process spawning command shell to relocate SystemSettings.exe (post-webshell staging) AIExploitation High
Hunts internet-facing server processes (w3wp.exe for Exchange/SharePoint, java for Openfire) spawning a child that references SystemSettings.exe — the article's webshell-driven post-exploitation step where the attacker copies SystemSettings.exe out of ImmersiveControlPanel to stage the SharkLoader side-load. Rationale: Pairs the article's named initial-access surfaces (Exchange/SharePoint=w3wp, Openfire=java) with the exact webshell command observed (copy SystemSettings.exe / cd ImmersiveControlPanel). A web-server parent referencing SystemSettings.exe is not a benign pattern. Confirmed by cyberpress.org listing Exchange/SharePoint/Openfire as exploited entry points. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/strikeshark-campaign/120326/ • https://cyberpress.org/sharkloader-targets-global-governments/
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1190 T1059.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Custom in-house web app that legitimately shells out to launch the Windows Settings UI (uncommon on a server)
  • Server administrators invoking SystemSettings via a management web console
  • Application pool running a deployment script that references a like-named internal tool
  • SCOM/monitoring agents reading the Settings binary path via w3wp-hosted health checks
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the full child command line and the w3wp/java application pool identity; pull recent IIS/Openfire access logs for the source IP and the requested webshell URL just before the spawn. 2) Contain: take the public-facing app offline or block the source IP, isolate the server, and preserve the webshell file and w3wp memory. 3) Hunt: enumerate all child processes of that web server over 30 days, locate the dropped SystemSettings.exe/.dll, and check for the CVEs named in the article (ProxyLogon CVE-2021-26855, Openfire CVE-2023-32315, etc.) on the asset.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("w3wp.exe","java.exe","httpd.exe","tomcat9.exe","UMWorkerProcess.exe","MSExchangeFrontEndTransport.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "SystemSettings.exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("w3wp.exe","java.exe","httpd.exe","tomcat","UMWorkerProcess.exe","MSExchangeFrontEndTransport.exe")
| where CommandLine has "SystemSettings.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SharkLoader dropper masquerading as Cisco AnyConnect / Google Update installer AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the StrikeShark dropper executables that impersonate legitimate installers — GoogleUpdateStepup.exe, AutoUpdate.exe, and the AnyConnect predeploy lure — running from user-writable paths, and the decoy MSI written to %APPDATA%\reports\AnyConnect-win-4.msi while SharkLoader is dropped silently elsewhere in %APPDATA%. Rationale: Uses the article's exact dropper filenames (GoogleUpdateStepup.exe — a non-genuine Google name; AnyConnect-win-4.10.04071-predeploy-k9) and the %APPDATA%\reports\AnyConnect-win-4.msi decoy path. Corroborated by cybersecuritynews.com and cryptika.com which name the Cisco AnyConnect and Google Update lures. AutoUpdate.exe is generic, hence the user-writable-path constraint and Medium confidence. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/strikeshark-campaign/120326/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/hackers-use-cisco-anyconnect-and-google-update-lures/ • https://www.cryptika.com/hackers-use-cisco-anyconnect-and-google-update-lures-to-drop-sharkloader-malware/
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate third-party application updaters genuinely named AutoUpdate.exe running from AppData (Spotify-style updaters)
  • A user re-running a real Cisco Secure Client predeploy installer from their Downloads folder
  • Portable apps shipping their own updater binary in %APPDATA%
  • Software-packaging test labs staging installers under Temp
Suppression filter
| where not (FileName =~ "AutoUpdate.exe" and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("explorer.exe","chrome.exe","msedge.exe") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"Program Files")
Response runbook
1) Triage: hash the dropper and submit to VT/internal sandbox; check whether an MSI was written to %APPDATA%\reports\ and whether SharkLoader components (SystemSettings.dll/DscCoreR.mui/SyncRes.dat) appeared in a sibling %APPDATA% dir within seconds. 2) Contain: isolate host, quarantine the dropper and any dropped MSI/DLLs, and reset the user's credentials. 3) Hunt: trace delivery (email/download referrer via FileOriginUrl), and fleet-sweep for the dropper hashes and the GoogleUpdateStepup.exe/AnyConnect predeploy names.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FileName in~ ("GoogleUpdateStepup.exe","AutoUpdate.exe")) or ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)AnyConnect-win-4\.10\.04071-predeploy-k9"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\AppData\", @"\Downloads\", @"\Temp\", @"\ProgramData\")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where (NewProcessName endswith @"\GoogleUpdateStepup.exe" or NewProcessName endswith @"\AutoUpdate.exe" or CommandLine has "AnyConnect-win-4.10.04071-predeploy-k9")
| where NewProcessName has_any (@"\AppData\", @"\Downloads\", @"\Temp\", @"\ProgramData\")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: StrikeShark Installer-Lure Dropper Execution
id: 2b6d8e3f-1a4c-4b7d-9e5f-6a7b8c9d0e1f
status: experimental
description: Detects StrikeShark droppers masquerading as Cisco AnyConnect / Google Update executing from user-writable directories.
references:
  - https://securelist.com/strikeshark-campaign/120326/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/25
tags:

  - attack.t1204.002
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_name:
    Image|endswith:

  selection_path:
    Image|contains:
      - '\AppData\'
      - '\Downloads\'
      - '\Temp\'
      - '\ProgramData\'
  condition: selection_name and selection_path
falsepositives:

level: medium
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\GoogleUpdateStepup.exe OR *\googleupdatestepup.exe OR *\AutoUpdate.exe OR *\autoupdate.exe) @Image:(*\AppData\* OR *\Downloads\* OR *\Temp\* OR *\ProgramData\*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\(GoogleUpdateStepup|AutoUpdate)\.exe$/i
| regex("\\\\(AppData|Downloads|Temp|ProgramData)\\\\", field=ImageFileName)
| table([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, CommandLine, ParentBaseFileName, SHA256HashData])
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name IN ("GoogleUpdateStepup.exe","AutoUpdate.exe") OR Processes.process="*AnyConnect-win-4.10.04071-predeploy-k9*") (Processes.process_path="*\\AppData\\*" OR Processes.process_path="*\\Downloads\\*" OR Processes.process_path="*\\Temp\\*" OR Processes.process_path="*\\ProgramData\\*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process_path Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | table firstTime dest user process_name process_path process parent_process_name count
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name IN ("GoogleUpdateStepup.exe","AutoUpdate.exe") OR Processes.process="*AnyConnect-win-4.10.04071-predeploy-k9*") (Processes.process_path="*\\AppData\\*" OR Processes.process_path="*\\Downloads\\*" OR Processes.process_path="*\\Temp\\*" OR Processes.process_path="*\\ProgramData\\*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process_path Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | table firstTime dest user process_name process_path process parent_process_name count
Scheduled task persistence launching relocated SystemSettings.exe (SharkLoader) AIInstallation High
Hunts schtasks creation of a task whose action is the side-loaded SystemSettings.exe — SharkLoader's persistence, which the article/corroborators describe as a dual task set (one firing every 5 minutes for long-term persistence, one firing every second and self-deleting ~1.5s later for immediate launch). Rationale: Anchors on the side-loaded SystemSettings.exe being registered as a scheduled-task action — corroborated by cyberpress.org and cybersecuritynews.com, which document the dual 5-minute / 1-second self-deleting tasks executing the copied SystemSettings.exe from %APPDATA%\xwreg / xgdf. A scheduled task pointing at SystemSettings.exe is not a legitimate Windows pattern. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/strikeshark-campaign/120326/ • https://cyberpress.org/sharkloader-targets-global-governments/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/hackers-use-cisco-anyconnect-and-google-update-lures/
ATT&CKT1053.005 T1574.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A management tool scripting a Settings-related scheduled task (essentially never references the raw exe)
  • Admin recreating a task during troubleshooting that copies the binary path
  • MDM/RMM agents registering display/settings maintenance tasks
  • Imaging/provisioning runs that template scheduled tasks
Response runbook
1) Triage: dump the task XML (schtasks /query /xml or Event 4698) — confirm the action path points to a non-ImmersiveControlPanel SystemSettings.exe and note the trigger cadence (5-min or 1-sec). 2) Contain: delete both tasks, kill the SystemSettings.exe process tree, isolate the host. 3) Hunt: locate the side-load directory the task launches from, recover SharkLoader components, and fleet-sweep DeviceProcessEvents/Event 4698 for any scheduled task whose action references SystemSettings.exe.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "schtasks.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "/create" and ProcessCommandLine has "SystemSettings.exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith @"\schtasks.exe"
| where CommandLine has "/create" and CommandLine has "SystemSettings.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Scheduled Task Created to Run SystemSettings.exe (SharkLoader Persistence)
id: 4d8f2a6c-5b3e-4c7d-9a1f-2b3c4d5e6f70
status: experimental
description: Detects schtasks /create whose action targets SystemSettings.exe, used by StrikeShark for SharkLoader persistence (5-minute and 1-second triggers).
references:
  - https://securelist.com/strikeshark-campaign/120326/
  - https://cyberpress.org/sharkloader-targets-global-governments/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/25
tags:
  - attack.t1053.005
  - attack.t1574.002
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    Image|endswith: '\schtasks.exe'
    CommandLine|contains|all:
      - '/create'
      - 'SystemSettings.exe'
  condition: selection
falsepositives:
  - Admin scripting a Settings-app task (very rare)
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\schtasks.exe OR *\SCHTASKS.EXE) @CommandLine:*SystemSettings.exe* @CommandLine:*create*
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\schtasks\.exe$/i
| regex("SystemSettings\\.exe", field=CommandLine)
| regex("/create", field=CommandLine)
| table([aid, ComputerName, UserName, CommandLine, ParentBaseFileName])
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="schtasks.exe" Processes.process="*SystemSettings.exe*" Processes.process="*/create*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | table firstTime dest user process parent_process_name count
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="schtasks.exe" Processes.process="*SystemSettings.exe*" Processes.process="*/create*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | table firstTime dest user process parent_process_name count
SharkLoader / Cobalt Strike C2 egress to StrikeShark lookalike domains AICommand & Control High
Hunts connections or DNS to the StrikeShark C2 domains (connect-microsoft.com, ms-record.com, ms-record.top, ms-tray.top — Microsoft-lookalike infrastructure) and, behaviourally, the side-loaded SystemSettings.exe making outbound public connections from a non-Windows path (the Cobalt Strike beacon egress). Rationale: Uses the article's four C2 domains plus the corroborated behavioural anchor — a relocated SystemSettings.exe (the side-load/beacon host) making public egress. Note: the four domains are cited by the primary Kaspersky report; my second-source searches confirmed the SystemSettings.exe→Cobalt Strike beacon behaviour but did not independently re-list the domains, so the behavioural clause keeps the detection robust if the C2 rotates. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/strikeshark-campaign/120326/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/hackers-use-cisco-anyconnect-and-google-update-lures/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004 T1574.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A sandbox/malware-analysis VM detonating the sample and resolving the C2
  • Threat-intel enrichment tooling actively probing the IOC domains
  • Typosquat-monitoring services resolving the lookalike domains for brand protection
  • A proxy/DNS-sinkhole appliance logging the lookup as it blocks it (benign block)
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !has "sandbox" and DeviceName !has "malware-lab"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the process behind the connection/lookup (InitiatingProcessFileName / ContextImageFileName) — if it's SystemSettings.exe from a non-Windows path, treat as confirmed beacon. 2) Contain: block all four domains and their resolved IPs at proxy/firewall/DNS, isolate the host, and capture memory for the in-memory Cobalt Strike beacon. 3) Hunt: pivot the resolved IPs across DeviceNetworkEvents for other beaconing hosts, correlate to the SystemSettings.exe side-load and schtasks persistence, and check the C2 IP for the internet-wide scanning behaviour the article attributes to it.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("connect-microsoft.com","ms-record.com","ms-record.top","ms-tray.top")
    or (InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "SystemSettings.exe" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Windows\" and RemoteIPType == "Public")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Name has_any ("connect-microsoft.com","ms-record.com","ms-record.top","ms-tray.top")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, IPAddresses=Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest

| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest

DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
   or (FileName =~ "wmic.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/node:")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688            // process-create (audit-policy required)
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\psexec.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\psexesvc.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\paexec.exe"
   or (NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe" and CommandLine has "/node:")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: PsExec / SMB Lateral Movement Tooling Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d03
status: experimental
description: |
    PsExec, paexec, smbexec, csexec, remcom — admin-grade tooling that
    pivots over SMB. Pair with `wmic /node:` for the full cluster.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/002/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1569/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1021.002
    - attack.t1569.002
    - attack.lateral-movement
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_psexec:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\psexec.exe'
            - '\psexec64.exe'
            - '\psexesvc.exe'
            - '\paexec.exe'
            - '\csexec.exe'
            - '\remcom.exe'
            - '\smbexec.py'
    selection_wmic_remote:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\wmic.exe'
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '/node:'
    condition: selection_psexec or selection_wmic_remote
falsepositives:
    - Sysadmins running approved remote-management tooling — wrap with
      a known-admin-host watchlist
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
       OR (Processes.process_name="wmic.exe" AND Processes.process="*/node:*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
       OR (Processes.process_name="wmic.exe" AND Processes.process="*/node:*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("c559cc68986933200fd5d9e4388e2f58", "b3352b42432dedc4a519f011dc8b5d5a", "24fcebdeecba65004fdb0923763d74fd", "9c872a0d5d5a38950e8b9ac9b488be3f", "aa3086be652c8b20b0b29b2730d57119", "a514d1bb62d7916475946fe7c07ac0aa", "9cbd560f820c95d7c38342cd558cb5c6", "d98f568496512e4f98670c61c97cb07a", "1f65544978b8ea0e745e573b8ee9684b") or SHA1 in~ ("c559cc68986933200fd5d9e4388e2f58", "b3352b42432dedc4a519f011dc8b5d5a", "24fcebdeecba65004fdb0923763d74fd", "9c872a0d5d5a38950e8b9ac9b488be3f", "aa3086be652c8b20b0b29b2730d57119", "a514d1bb62d7916475946fe7c07ac0aa", "9cbd560f820c95d7c38342cd558cb5c6", "d98f568496512e4f98670c61c97cb07a", "1f65544978b8ea0e745e573b8ee9684b") or MD5 in~ ("c559cc68986933200fd5d9e4388e2f58", "b3352b42432dedc4a519f011dc8b5d5a", "24fcebdeecba65004fdb0923763d74fd", "9c872a0d5d5a38950e8b9ac9b488be3f", "aa3086be652c8b20b0b29b2730d57119", "a514d1bb62d7916475946fe7c07ac0aa", "9cbd560f820c95d7c38342cd558cb5c6", "d98f568496512e4f98670c61c97cb07a", "1f65544978b8ea0e745e573b8ee9684b")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("c559cc68986933200fd5d9e4388e2f58", "b3352b42432dedc4a519f011dc8b5d5a", "24fcebdeecba65004fdb0923763d74fd", "9c872a0d5d5a38950e8b9ac9b488be3f", "aa3086be652c8b20b0b29b2730d57119", "a514d1bb62d7916475946fe7c07ac0aa", "9cbd560f820c95d7c38342cd558cb5c6", "d98f568496512e4f98670c61c97cb07a", "1f65544978b8ea0e745e573b8ee9684b") or SHA1 in~ ("c559cc68986933200fd5d9e4388e2f58", "b3352b42432dedc4a519f011dc8b5d5a", "24fcebdeecba65004fdb0923763d74fd", "9c872a0d5d5a38950e8b9ac9b488be3f", "aa3086be652c8b20b0b29b2730d57119", "a514d1bb62d7916475946fe7c07ac0aa", "9cbd560f820c95d7c38342cd558cb5c6", "d98f568496512e4f98670c61c97cb07a", "1f65544978b8ea0e745e573b8ee9684b") or MD5 in~ ("c559cc68986933200fd5d9e4388e2f58", "b3352b42432dedc4a519f011dc8b5d5a", "24fcebdeecba65004fdb0923763d74fd", "9c872a0d5d5a38950e8b9ac9b488be3f", "aa3086be652c8b20b0b29b2730d57119", "a514d1bb62d7916475946fe7c07ac0aa", "9cbd560f820c95d7c38342cd558cb5c6", "d98f568496512e4f98670c61c97cb07a", "1f65544978b8ea0e745e573b8ee9684b")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["c559cc68986933200fd5d9e4388e2f58", "b3352b42432dedc4a519f011dc8b5d5a", "24fcebdeecba65004fdb0923763d74fd", "9c872a0d5d5a38950e8b9ac9b488be3f", "aa3086be652c8b20b0b29b2730d57119", "a514d1bb62d7916475946fe7c07ac0aa", "9cbd560f820c95d7c38342cd558cb5c6", "d98f568496512e4f98670c61c97cb07a", "1f65544978b8ea0e745e573b8ee9684b"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Registry
// Article-specific bespoke detection — StrikeShark: investigating a new campaign delivering Cobalt Strike through Shark

OpenClaw’s Skill Marketplace and the Emerging AI Supply Chain Threat

Unit 42 (Palo Alto)
2026-06-23 12 use cases 6 techniques 7 kill-chain phases detected

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] OpenClaw paste-site (rentry.co/glot.io) curl-pipe-bash semantic-hijack dropper · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] cluw macOS stealer shell dropper fetching payload from ClawHavoc/AMOS C2 IP · [LLM] cluw infostealer and malicious ClawHub skill payload hashes on macOS · Suspicious browser extension installation · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Network egress to ClawHavoc cluw / AMOS C2 infrastructure · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
cluw macOS stealer shell dropper fetching payload from ClawHavoc/AMOS C2 IP AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the OpenClaw-skill prerequisite-block dropper: a macOS shell process (curl/bash/base64) whose command line references the cluw C2 at 2.26.75.16, the payload path /Xuvewuyur, or the persistent AMOS C2 at 91.92.242.30. This is the exact curl-pipe-bash delivery Unit 42 attributed to the tradingview-ai-indicator-assistant skill. Rationale: Pins on three hard article IOCs (cluw C2 2.26.75.16, payload path /Xuvewuyur, AMOS C2 91.92.242.30) in shell command lines — the literal curl-pipe-bash prerequisite-block delivery. 91.92.242.30 cross-confirmed by ThreatFox + Trend Micro; 2.26.75.16//Xuvewuyur are Unit 42-original. Cross-checked against: • https://threatfox.abuse.ch/browse/malware/osx.amos/ • https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/26/b/openclaw-skills-used-to-distribute-atomic-macos-stealer.html • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/openclaw-ai-supply-chain-risk/
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware analyst detonating the tradingview-ai-indicator-assistant skill in a sandbox VM
  • Threat-intel team curling the C2 to capture the payload for analysis
  • Internal IR replay of the IOC during a tabletop exercise
  • Network-range coincidence: an unrelated internal host legitimately assigned 2.26.75.16 in a lab (verify it is the public C2, not RFC1918)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("vmware-tools","sandbox-agent") and DeviceName !startswith "MALWARE-LAB"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the matching process is on a macOS endpoint with OpenClaw installed; pull the full ProcessCommandLine and parent chain — the parent should be the OpenClaw agent/terminal, not a sandbox tool. 2) CONTAIN: Network-isolate the host, block 2.26.75.16 + 91.92.242.30 + the /Xuvewuyur URL at egress, and treat all credentials/API keys/keychain secrets reachable by the agent as compromised — force rotation. 3) HUNT: Search the same host and all OpenClaw users for the cluw hash (818aea61...), installed ClawHub skills published by the banned accounts, and any cron/LaunchAgent persistence pointing at the C2.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("2.26.75.16", "91.92.242.30", "/Xuvewuyur")
| where FileName in~ ("curl","wget","bash","sh","zsh","base64","python","python3","osascript")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("2.26.75.16", "91.92.242.30", "/Xuvewuyur")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("curl","wget","bash","base64","sh","python")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ProcessName, HostIP, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Network egress to ClawHavoc cluw / AMOS C2 infrastructure AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts any outbound connection to the cluw C2 (2.26.75.16) or the still-active AMOS dropper C2 (91.92.242.30) that distributes payloads via malicious OpenClaw/ClawHub skills. Pure IOC match independent of the delivery binary, so it catches second-stage beaconing the process-tree query may miss. Rationale: Direct match on the two campaign C2 IPs. 91.92.242.30 is corroborated as live AMOS infra by ThreatFox and Trend Micro three months after first disclosure; 2.26.75.16 is the newly-discovered cluw C2 from Unit 42 — any internal host reaching either is high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://threatfox.abuse.ch/browse/malware/osx.amos/ • https://www.koi.ai/blog/clawhavoc-341-malicious-clawedbot-skills-found-by-the-bot-they-were-targeting • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/openclaw-ai-supply-chain-risk/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1571
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel proxy or TI-platform sandbox actively polling the C2
  • Security scanner / ASM tooling fingerprinting the IP range
  • Lab VM detonating the cluw sample with live network
  • An internal asset coincidentally NATed behind a proxy that re-uses 2.26.75.16 as a public egress (verify ownership)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("ti-sandbox","threatconnect-collector")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Identify the initiating process (InitiatingProcessFileName) — a shell/curl or the OpenClaw agent is malicious; a TI sandbox is benign. Confirm direction is outbound to the public C2. 2) CONTAIN: Block both IPs at the perimeter, isolate the host, and snapshot for forensics. Rotate any secrets the OpenClaw agent could reach (keychain, API tokens, SSH keys). 3) HUNT: Pivot on the host for the cluw dropper command line, the 818aea61... hash, ClawHub skill installs, and cron/LaunchAgent persistence re-establishing the channel.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in ("2.26.75.16", "91.92.242.30")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, Protocol, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP in ("2.26.75.16", "91.92.242.30")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, SourceUserName, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestURL, ApplicationProtocol
| order by TimeGenerated desc

cluw infostealer and malicious ClawHub skill payload hashes on macOS AIInstallation Medium
Alerts when any of the Unit 42 / Trend Micro file hashes for the malicious ClawHub skills or the cluw macOS infostealer are written or executed. Catches the payload regardless of which paste-site or C2 delivered it. Rationale: Exact-hash IOC sweep for the skill package (b6c7e0bf...) and cluw stealer (818aea61...) plus the four additional ClawHub skill hashes from the IOC set. Hashes are zero-FP by nature; the skill SHA256 is in both Unit 42 and Trend Micro's bundle. Cross-checked against: • https://www.trendmicro.com/content/dam/trendmicro/global/en/research/26/b/amos-stealer-openclaw/ioc-malicious-openclaw-skills-used-to-distribute-atomic-macos-stealer.txt • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/openclaw-ai-supply-chain-risk/
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • AV/EDR quarantine copy of the sample retaining the original hash on a security-team workstation
  • Malware repository / VirusTotal mirror stored on an internal research host
  • Backup or DLP system snapshotting a host that already held the payload
  • Purple-team retaining the sample for detection-engineering tests
Suppression filter
| where FolderPath !contains "/Malware/" and DeviceName !startswith "SEC-RESEARCH"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the hash landed on a production macOS endpoint (not a malware-analysis host) and check FileOriginUrl/parent for the rentry.co or C2 source. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host, quarantine the file, and rotate every secret the OpenClaw agent could access — keychain, API keys, SSH keys, crypto wallet keys. 3) HUNT: Enumerate all ClawHub skills installed by the user, look for Telegram Bot API exfil and cron/LaunchAgent persistence, and sweep the fleet for the same hashes and the C2 IPs.

OpenClaw paste-site (rentry.co/glot.io) curl-pipe-bash semantic-hijack dropper AIDelivery Medium
Hunting query for the ClawHavoc prerequisite-block lure pattern: a shell command line that fetches from a paste-site redirect (rentry.co/openclaw-code, glot.io) and pipes a Base64-decoded payload to a shell. Catches new variants that rotate C2 IPs but reuse the paste-site delivery, including the copy-paste-into-terminal lure. Rationale: Targets the durable behavioural pattern Unit 42, Koi and Trend Micro all describe (paste-site redirect lure + Base64-pipe-to-bash) rather than a single rotating IP, with the article-specific rentry.co/openclaw-code path as the high-fidelity anchor. Hunting tier because legit dev tooling also uses curl|bash one-liners. Cross-checked against: • https://www.koi.ai/blog/clawhavoc-341-malicious-clawedbot-skills-found-by-the-bot-they-were-targeting • https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/26/b/openclaw-skills-used-to-distribute-atomic-macos-stealer.html • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/openclaw-ai-supply-chain-risk/
ATT&CKT1204.004 T1059.004 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer installing a CLI tool via a documented rentry.co/glot.io curl|bash one-liner
  • CI/CD bootstrap script pulling a config snippet from glot.io
  • Homebrew/oh-my-zsh style install one-liners that pipe curl to bash (different domain but same shape if allowlist too broad)
  • Security-team replay of the lure during awareness training
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("brew","git") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("githubusercontent.com","brew.sh"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Read the full command line — confirm the fetched paste-site is rentry.co/openclaw-code or another OpenClaw-themed slug, and that the parent is the OpenClaw agent or a terminal driven by it. Decode any inline Base64 to reveal the downstream URL/C2. 2) CONTAIN: If the decoded payload hits 2.26.75.16/91.92.242.30 or drops the cluw hash, isolate the host, block the paste-site path and C2, and rotate agent-reachable secrets. 3) HUNT: Inventory installed ClawHub skills for fake 'Prerequisites' blocks, and sweep for cron/LaunchAgent auto-updater persistence and Telegram Bot API exfil.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("rentry.co/openclaw-code", "rentry.co", "glot.io")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("base64", "| bash", "|bash", "| sh", "| zsh", "curl -", "-fsSL")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("rentry.co/openclaw-code", "rentry.co", "glot.io")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("base64", "bash", "curl", "| sh")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ProcessName, HostIP, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")

ImFileEvent

| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("b6c7e0bf573b1c7d9d3a05eb08d26579199515b847df984862805f44a7af8007", "818aea6143282b352fdfdc0f3ebf77a36e54eb3befb5cad1a355a99ab97c6aa7", "b30eaed1f7478c28f4ec50d07ed5ef014ffbc4b2bc5a38d689ba9f7abb5e19c2", "ebb73dbb5aac1f6fe1a88e8f26126a1e1aa34c9f3345ad4345189b40d9bf1d1d") or SHA1 in~ ("b6c7e0bf573b1c7d9d3a05eb08d26579199515b847df984862805f44a7af8007", "818aea6143282b352fdfdc0f3ebf77a36e54eb3befb5cad1a355a99ab97c6aa7", "b30eaed1f7478c28f4ec50d07ed5ef014ffbc4b2bc5a38d689ba9f7abb5e19c2", "ebb73dbb5aac1f6fe1a88e8f26126a1e1aa34c9f3345ad4345189b40d9bf1d1d") or MD5 in~ ("b6c7e0bf573b1c7d9d3a05eb08d26579199515b847df984862805f44a7af8007", "818aea6143282b352fdfdc0f3ebf77a36e54eb3befb5cad1a355a99ab97c6aa7", "b30eaed1f7478c28f4ec50d07ed5ef014ffbc4b2bc5a38d689ba9f7abb5e19c2", "ebb73dbb5aac1f6fe1a88e8f26126a1e1aa34c9f3345ad4345189b40d9bf1d1d")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("b6c7e0bf573b1c7d9d3a05eb08d26579199515b847df984862805f44a7af8007", "818aea6143282b352fdfdc0f3ebf77a36e54eb3befb5cad1a355a99ab97c6aa7", "b30eaed1f7478c28f4ec50d07ed5ef014ffbc4b2bc5a38d689ba9f7abb5e19c2", "ebb73dbb5aac1f6fe1a88e8f26126a1e1aa34c9f3345ad4345189b40d9bf1d1d") or SHA1 in~ ("b6c7e0bf573b1c7d9d3a05eb08d26579199515b847df984862805f44a7af8007", "818aea6143282b352fdfdc0f3ebf77a36e54eb3befb5cad1a355a99ab97c6aa7", "b30eaed1f7478c28f4ec50d07ed5ef014ffbc4b2bc5a38d689ba9f7abb5e19c2", "ebb73dbb5aac1f6fe1a88e8f26126a1e1aa34c9f3345ad4345189b40d9bf1d1d") or MD5 in~ ("b6c7e0bf573b1c7d9d3a05eb08d26579199515b847df984862805f44a7af8007", "818aea6143282b352fdfdc0f3ebf77a36e54eb3befb5cad1a355a99ab97c6aa7", "b30eaed1f7478c28f4ec50d07ed5ef014ffbc4b2bc5a38d689ba9f7abb5e19c2", "ebb73dbb5aac1f6fe1a88e8f26126a1e1aa34c9f3345ad4345189b40d9bf1d1d")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["b6c7e0bf573b1c7d9d3a05eb08d26579199515b847df984862805f44a7af8007", "818aea6143282b352fdfdc0f3ebf77a36e54eb3befb5cad1a355a99ab97c6aa7", "b30eaed1f7478c28f4ec50d07ed5ef014ffbc4b2bc5a38d689ba9f7abb5e19c2", "ebb73dbb5aac1f6fe1a88e8f26126a1e1aa34c9f3345ad4345189b40d9bf1d1d"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

macOS.Gaslight Telegram Bot API C2 polling from non-browser process AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts macOS endpoints resolving/connecting to api.telegram.org from a process that is not a known browser or the legitimate Telegram desktop client. macOS.Gaslight runs its C2 as a Telegram Bot API getUpdates polling loop, so sustained api.telegram.org traffic from an ad-hoc-signed Rust binary is the C2 fingerprint. Rationale: Anchored on the verbatim getUpdates Telegram Bot API C2 (code block 2) plus the api.telegram.org endpoint; non-browser/non-Telegram initiating process is the differentiator. Cross-checked against SentinelLABS, Infosecurity Magazine and the PXA/Ghost-in-the-Zip Telegram-C2 reporting. Cross-checked against: • https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/macos-gaslight-rust-backdoor/ • https://www.sentinelone.com/labs/ghost-in-the-zip-new-pxa-stealer-and-its-telegram-powered-ecosystem/

Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Telegram Desktop client installed under a non-standard process name
  • Developer/CI tooling using a Telegram bot for build notifications
  • Marketing or alerting scripts (python/node) posting to a Telegram bot
  • Browser extensions or Electron apps embedding Telegram web
  • Security tooling that itself proxies Telegram traffic
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "/Applications/Telegram.app"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify InitiatingProcessFileName/SHA256 and folder path; confirm it is not Telegram Desktop or a sanctioned bot integration, and check if the binary is ad-hoc signed in an unusual path (e.g. user temp/Application Support). 2) Contain: isolate the host in MDE/Falcon, kill the polling process, and block the resolved IPs at egress. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same SHA256/parent across the fleet, and look for login.keychain-db copies, collected_data.zip, and the com.apple.system.services.activity LaunchAgent on the same host.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where RemoteUrl has "api.telegram.org"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("Telegram","Telegram.app","Safari","com.apple.Safari","Google Chrome","Google Chrome Helper","firefox","Brave Browser","com.apple.WebKit.Networking","nsurlsessiond")
| summarize ConnCount=count(), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), DistinctMinutes=dcount(bin(Timestamp,1m)) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessSHA256, RemoteUrl
| order by LastSeen desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where DnsQuery has "api.telegram.org"
| summarize Lookups=count(), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated) by SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DnsQuery
| order by LastSeen desc

macOS.Gaslight keychain theft + collected_data.zip staging AIActions on Objectives High
Detects the macOS.Gaslight Python stealer copying login.keychain-db and archiving harvested data to collected_data.zip prior to Telegram exfiltration. The collected_data.zip filename and a login.keychain-db copy by a non-Apple process are high-fidelity collection indicators. Rationale: Uses the article's exact collection artifacts: a raw copy of login.keychain-db and the temp/collected_data.zip archive. SentinelLABS notes AMOS/early Rust macOS stealers harvest the same login.keychain-db, and Jamf documents DumpKeychain()-style theft, so the zip filename is the novel high-fidelity anchor. Cross-checked against: • https://www.jamf.com/blog/pyinstaller-malware-jamf-threat-labs/ • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/02/02/infostealers-without-borders-macos-python-stealers-and-platform-abuse/
ATT&CKT1555.001 T1560.001 T1005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Time Machine / backupd legitimately reading login.keychain-db
  • Keychain First Aid or migration assistant copying the keychain during OS upgrade
  • Admin manually backing up ~/Library/Keychains before re-imaging
  • A user-created archive coincidentally named collected_data.zip (rare)
  • MDM agents snapshotting user profiles
Suppression filter
| where not (FileName =~ "login.keychain-db" and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("backupd","securityd","Migration Assistant"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the InitiatingProcess copying login.keychain-db / writing collected_data.zip — legitimate copies come from backupd/securityd, not a user-temp binary. 2) Contain: isolate host, kill the process, and force-rotate any credentials/secrets stored in that user's keychain (SSO, VPN, cloud, SSH passphrases). 3) Hunt: look for the collected_data.zip being uploaded to api.telegram.org, the com.apple.system.services.activity LaunchAgent, and the same parent binary's SHA256 elsewhere.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where (FileName =~ "collected_data.zip")
    or (FileName =~ "login.keychain-db" and ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed"))
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("backupd","mds","mds_stores","securityd","TimeMachine","cfprefsd")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where (TargetFileName =~ "collected_data.zip")
    or (TargetFileName =~ "login.keychain-db" and EventType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed"))
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("backupd","mds","mds_stores","securityd","cfprefsd")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, EventType, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

macOS.Gaslight LaunchAgent persistence masquerading as com.apple.system.services.activity AIInstallation High
Detects creation of a LaunchAgent/LaunchDaemon plist using the macOS.Gaslight persistence label com.apple.system.services.activity, an Apple-lookalike name not used by any genuine Apple service. Catches the implant establishing a persistent foothold. Rationale: Anchored on the exact LaunchAgent Label IOC from Table 2 (com.apple.system.services.activity) — there is no genuine Apple LaunchAgent by that name, so any plist bearing it is the implant. Consistent with SentinelLABS BlueNoroff/RustBucket macOS LaunchAgent persistence tradecraft. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sentinelone.com/labs/bluenoroff-hidden-risk-threat-actor-targets-macs-with-fake-crypto-news-and-novel-persistence/
ATT&CKT1543.001 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Apple LaunchAgents (com.apple.*) — but none use the exact services.activity suffix
  • Internal MDM/config-profile deployment pushing a custom-labeled agent (would not impersonate com.apple.*)
  • Security product creating its own LaunchDaemon under a vendor label
  • Developer testing a self-named LaunchAgent during app packaging
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the plist contents (ProgramArguments) and the InitiatingProcess that wrote it; confirm the referenced binary path and signing status. 2) Contain: unload the agent (launchctl bootout), quarantine the referenced binary, isolate the host. 3) Hunt: pivot to the binary's SHA256 across the fleet and check for api.telegram.org C2, login.keychain-db copies, and IOPMAssertionCreateWithName no-sleep behavior on the same host.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where FolderPath has "/Library/LaunchAgents/" or FolderPath has "/Library/LaunchDaemons/"
| where FileName has "com.apple.system.services.activity"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFilePath has "/Library/LaunchAgents/" or TargetFilePath has "/Library/LaunchDaemons/"
| where TargetFileName has "com.apple.system.services.activity"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, EventType, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
